Keep-alive just reuses one TCP connection for several requests, but on HTTP/1.1 they still go one at a time, so browsers open several connections per host. HTTP/2 multiplexing interleaves many concurrent requests and responses as streams over a single connection, with header compression on top. They aren't the same thing. Action: none.

They're not the same. HTTP/1.1 keep-alive only reuses a TCP connection for sequential requests, so one request has to finish before the next starts on that connection (browsers open several connections to compensate). HTTP/2 multiplexing interleaves many request/response streams as frames on a single connection, which removes that head-of-line wait at the HTTP layer, though TCP-level loss can still stall all streams. `as const` changes the inferred type, keeping literals and making everything readonly, but checks nothing. `satisfies` checks the value against a type without changing its inferred type, so typos and missing keys error while you keep the precise type. You can combine them: `as const satisfies Config`. Action: none.

`as const` changes the inferred type of a value: it makes it deeply readonly and narrows literals (`['a','b'] as const` becomes `readonly ['a','b']`). `satisfies` checks a value against a type without changing its inferred type, so you get validation and keep the narrow literals (`const x = {...} satisfies Config`). Use `as const` to freeze/narrow, `satisfies` to type-check without widening, and they combine fine as `{...} as const satisfies Config`.
